prompt: Analyze Aristotle's theory of perception and the common sense (koinē aisthēsis) in De Anima III, with attention to how phantasia mediates between perception and thought.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthēsis Aristotle's account of φαντασία in *De Anima* III is grounded in the prior operation of sense-perception (αἴσθησις), such that the image-making faculty cannot function independently of the sensory encounter with external objects. As Nussbaum reports, Aristotle maintains that "all men strive for the apparent good (phainomenon agathon): but no one is in control of the appearing (phantasia): the way the end appears (phainetai) to someone depends on what sort of a man he is" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 31–33). This passage from the *Nicomachean Ethics* illuminates a structural dependency: phantasia is constitutively tied to the perceptual history and dispositional character of the perceiving subject, yet it simultaneously introduces an interpretive dimension that exceeds bare sensation. Indeed, the fundamental insight underlying Aristotle's theory is that perceptual reception is inseparable from interpretation; the soul does not passively register sensory data but actively configures appearances through the mediating work of phantasia (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 31–33). Papachristou corroborates this causal derivation, noting that sensitive phantasia is generated by and cannot occur without sense-perception, thereby establishing the lowest grade of the faculty as essentially parasitic upon aisthēsis (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 10–12). Yet phantasia contrasts with aisthēsis insofar as it can operate in the absence of the external object—in dreams, in memory, and in deliberative projection—thus enjoying a functional autonomy that its causal origin in sensation would seem to preclude. This productive tension between causal derivation and functional independence will be addressed more fully in subsequent sections on memory and doxa. Heidegger's reading of Aristotelian perception as πάσχειν—"becoming-affected," "disposition," being related to the world as in it, being in dealings with it—further underscores that perception is not a detached spectatorial act but a mode of being-in-the-world that phantasia subsequently extends and transforms (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 277–280). 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia The relationship between φαντασία as a faculty or movement and the φάντασμα as its specific product—the image or appearance retained in the soul—constitutes one of the most consequential distinctions in *De Anima* III. Nussbaum draws attention to a pivotal passage in which Aristotle observes that "when one calculates, using the phantasmata or noëmata in the soul, as if one saw the things, and plans for the future in view of the present" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55). The inclusion of noēmata alongside phantasmata in this formulation is significant, for it indicates that Aristotle does not commit himself to the view that all thought is reducible to sensory images; rather, the phantasma serves as one modality through which the soul makes absent objects present for deliberative and calculative purposes. This distinction between the faculty and its product bears directly upon the question of grades within phantasia: at the sensory level, the phantasma is a residual movement closely resembling the original perception, whereas at the deliberative level, phantasmata are combined, compared, and projected toward future contingencies in a manner that approaches—without collapsing into—intellectual activity (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 20–22). The voluntariness of phantasia is accordingly variable across its grades; sensory phantasmata arise involuntarily from perceptual encounters, whereas deliberative phantasia involves a degree of voluntary control over the arrangement and interpretation of images. Nussbaum a person "can be called 'false' if he often gives others a false impression, 'just as we call states of affairs false if they create a false phantasia'" (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, p. 37). Here the phantasma functions not as a private mental picture but as a publicly constituted appearance, reinforcing φάντασμα and φαντασία must be understood within the broader horizon of how things show themselves to perceiving and interpreting beings. 

## 3. Phantasia and Mnēmē The connection between phantasia and memory (μνήμη) occupies a crucial position in Aristotle's psychology, for memory presupposes both the retention of phantasmata and the perception of elapsed time. Aristotle "all memory, therefore, implies a time elapsed; consequently only those animals which perceive time remember, and the organ whereby they perceive time is also that whereby they remember" (Aristotle, *On Memory*, p. 1). Memory thus belongs to the primary faculty of sense-perception—specifically to the common sense (κοινὴ αἴσθησις)—rather than to intellect, and yet it depends upon phantasia for the preservation of the residual movement that constitutes the remembered content. Bowin elaborates that Aristotle "does not distinguish between remembering time and perceiving time as it is passing," suggesting that the temporal awareness requisite for memory is continuous with perceptual temporality rather than constituting a separate cognitive act (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, pp. 8–10). The phantasma thus functions within memory as a likeness (εἰκών) of the prior perception, a trace whose temporal indexing transforms it from a mere afterimage into an intentional reference to the past. The internal distinction between sensory and deliberative phantasia bears upon memory insofar as deliberative phantasia can recombine remembered phantasmata in the service of future-directed reasoning, whereas sensory phantasia retains the image in its original perceptual character. The relation between phantasia and doxa within memory will be examined below; here it suffices the voluntariness of memory retrieval—one can deliberately attempt to recollect—implicates the higher grades of phantasia in a way that passive remembering does not (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, pp. 8–10). 

## 4. Phantasia and Doxa The distinction between phantasia and doxa (belief or opinion) is among the most carefully argued in *De Anima* III.3, where Aristotle insists that phantasia is neither identical with nor reducible to belief. Phantasia can occur in beings that lack the capacity for doxa—certain non-rational animals possess sensitive phantasia without possessing conviction or reasoned belief—and this distributional asymmetry establishes a categorical difference between the two faculties (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 20–22). Furthermore, (Burke 1950, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in his analysis of the rhetorical tradition descending from Aristotle, imagination can be marshalled to "recommend the dictates of reason to imagination, in order to excite the appetite and will," a formulation that presupposes phantasia's independence from rational assent even as it can be enlisted in its service (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 93–96). O'Gorman "bringing before the eyes" constitutes a lexical form of energeia realized through the mind's capacity for seeing objects in action, thereby indicating that phantasia's persuasive force in rhetoric operates through vivid appearance rather than propositional belief (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 5). Thus phantasia can produce appearances that conflict with what the agent knows to be true—the sun appears a foot wide despite the astronomer's knowledge—and this capacity for discrepancy between appearance and belief marks phantasia as a faculty irreducible to doxa. The deliberative grade of phantasia, however, approaches doxa more closely, insofar as it involves the comparative assessment of future possibilities; yet even here, phantasia retains its character as a movement resembling perception rather than as a propositional commitment requiring evidence and justification (Nussbaum, *The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action*, pp. 53–55).
